summary:
I developed a Mars survival simulation game where players take on the role of an astronaut researching biology and radiation to build a new habitat. After a massive dust storm destroys the base, the sole survivor must race against time to repair communications and send research data back to the ISS before resources run out.
This game addresses the challenge of making complex space science engaging and accessible. Instead of reading dry textbooks, players actively experience the mechanics of surviving in the Goldilocks zone while managing real scientific missions.
This is important because it inspires curiosity about space exploration and teaches critical problem-solving and resource management skills through interactive storytelling.
details:
What it does & How it works:
Our project is a 2D web-based educational survival game set in South Utopia Planitia on Mars. Players take on the role of the sole surviving astronaut researcher after a massive dust storm destroys their habitat. Through an interactive, turn-based decision loop (with no time pressure), players manage four core resources—Energy, Oxygen, Parts, and Research—to explore real Martian landmarks, scavenge abandoned rovers and landers (like Spirit, Opportunity, and Viking), conduct biological and radiation research, and repair a communication tower to contact Earth and the ISS before their supplies run out.

Benefits & Intended Impact:
Designed specifically for children aged 7–12, the game transforms complex space science into an accessible, hands-on adventure. It seamlessly integrates all four pillars of STEM:

  • Science: Players uncover real facts about Mars' atmosphere, radiation, and environment to understand cause and effect.
  • Technology: Players interact with and salvage real-world historical Mars rovers and landers.
  • Engineering: Players gather scrap parts to craft survival tools and rebuild the communication tower step-by-step.
  • Mathematics: Players use critical thinking and basic math to calculate resource trade-offs, weigh risks, and align signal coordinates with Earth.

Our intended impact is to spark curiosity in space exploration, build critical problem-solving skills, and foster a growth mindset in young learners.

Creativity & Team Considerations:
To make the game engaging and age-appropriate for 7–12-year-olds, our team carefully considered cognitive load and emotional design:

  • Stress-Free Pacing: We intentionally avoided real-time timers and 3D open-world complexity so kids can read, calculate risks, and think at their own pace.
  • Constructive Failure: Instead of a discouraging "Game Over," running out of resources triggers an encouraging "Mission Aborted" screen with helpful scientific tips for their next attempt.
  • Transparent Cause & Effect: Every action clearly displays its resource cost upfront, teaching players that every decision has a logical consequence while unlocking multiple positive endings.
  • Atmosphere: We paired a cool-toned color palette with sci-fi ambient audio to immerse players in the Martian environment without overwhelming them.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used:

  • Game Development & Web: Visual Studio Code, Html
  • Design & Prototyping: Visual Studio Code, Gemini, Claude
